evidence.claim: Two Cascade passes link wagon routes, lava fields, rivers and forests.
evidence.quote: Lava fields, snowcapped peaks and rushing rivers mark this 82-mile loop around two of central Oregon's Cascade Mountain passes.

evidence.claim: wagon routes
evidence.quote: The Byway follows the path of an 1860s wagon route

evidence.claim: The McKenzie Pass–Santiam Pass Scenic Byway makes an 82-mile loop across two Cascade passes, through lava fields and forests.
evidence.quote: Lava fields, snowcapped peaks and rushing rivers mark this 82-mile loop around two of central Oregon's Cascade Mountain passes.

evidence.claim: Lodgepole pines prevail on the drier east side; Douglas fir and red cedar grow west of the crest.
evidence.quote: On the west side of the Cascades, you'll encounter lush Douglas fir and red cedar forests; on the drier east side, lodgepole pines prevail.

evidence.claim: ODOT allows three to five hours and identifies the volcanic and glacial landscapes as nationally significant features of the drive.
evidence.quote: Minimum Driving Time: 3-5 hours

evidence.claim: ODOT allows three to five hours and identifies the volcanic and glacial landscapes as nationally significant features of the drive.
evidence.quote: The natural qualities of the McKenzie Pass-Santiam Pass Scenic Byway are of national significance. There are outstanding examples of both ancient and recent volcanoes, cinder cones, lava flows, and deep, glaciated canyons.

evidence.claim: The route became a National Scenic Byway in 1998.
evidence.quote: before becoming a National Scenic Byway on  June 9, 1998.

evidence.claim: At McKenzie Pass, today’s highway follows a wagon route cut through lava beds.
evidence.quote: At the summit, the wagon road had to be cut through the lava beds.

evidence.claim: today’s highway follows a wagon route
evidence.quote: Today’s highway follows the wagon route over the lava beds past the observatory site.

evidence.claim: That difficult crossing sent most early travelers to alternate Cascade routes.
evidence.quote: As a result, alternate routes over the Cascades were used by most early travelers.

evidence.claim: In 1935, the Civilian Conservation Corps completed Dee Wright Observatory at the pass, building a shelter from lava found on the site.
evidence.quote: The observatory was built during the Great Depression by a Civilian Conservation Corps crew at Camp Belknap near Clear Lake. It was completed in 1935

evidence.claim: building a shelter from lava found on the site.
evidence.quote: The observatory is an open shelter built with basaltic andesite lava found at the construction site.

evidence.claim: Beginning in Sisters, take the loop west over Santiam Pass, then south along the McKenzie River valley toward Clear Lake.
evidence.quote: It follows Oregon Route 126 westward over Santiam Pass south of Three Fingered Jack, then south along the valley of the McKenzie River.

evidence.claim: Beginning in Sisters
evidence.quote: The route begins on its eastern end at the town of Sisters

evidence.claim: south along the McKenzie River valley toward Clear Lake.
evidence.quote: A few miles north of Clear Lake, Oregon Route 126 joins U.S. Route 20 and Oregon Route 22, and turns east toward the Santiam Pass and Sisters.

evidence.claim: Continue south past the river’s waterfalls before turning east on OR 242 toward Proxy Falls and McKenzie Pass.
evidence.quote: It then follows Oregon Route 242 eastward over McKenzie Pass

evidence.claim: Continue south past the river’s waterfalls
evidence.quote: A few miles up the highway turns into Koosah Falls. Here, a loop trail connects hikers to stunning Sahalie Falls and Carmen Reservoir.

evidence.claim: turning east on OR 242 toward Proxy Falls and McKenzie Pass.

evidence.claim: McKenzie Pass stands at 5,325 feet, with lava surrounding the road; Windy Point opens onto a 65-square-mile lava flow.
evidence.quote: emerging from the forest at Windy Point to a jaw-dropping vista of Mount Washington and a 65-square-mile lava flow. When you reach 5,325-foot McKenzie Pass, you're enveloped by lava on all sides.

evidence.claim: Beyond the lava at the summit, the highway returns to Sisters.
evidence.quote: eastward over McKenzie Pass, north of the Three Sisters then back to the town of Sisters.

evidence.claim: Clear Lake’s water takes a long route from mountain to lake.
evidence.quote: The runoff filters through caverns for more than 20 years before emptying into Clear Lake.

evidence.claim: Snow runoff from Mount Washington and nearby terrain supplies most of it, filtering through caverns for more than twenty years before arriving.
evidence.quote: The lake is primarily fed by snow runoff from nearby Mount Washington and the surrounding areas. The runoff filters through caverns for more than 20 years before emptying into Clear Lake.

evidence.claim: Below the surface is another measure of time: upright trees stand submerged 100 feet deep, killed approximately 3,000 years ago when volcanic activity formed the lake.
evidence.quote: Submerged 100 feet (30 m) deep in the lake is a stand of upright trees that were killed approximately 3,000 years ago when volcanic activity created the lake.

evidence.claim: Water stays between 35 and 43 degrees Fahrenheit year-round, preserving the submerged trees.
evidence.quote: The trees are remarkably preserved due to the cold year-round water temperatures of between 35–43 °F (2–6 °C).

evidence.claim: The lake forms the McKenzie River’s headwaters; water leaving its southern end goes on to Sahalie and Koosah falls.
evidence.quote: The south end of Clear Lake empties 250,000 gallons per minute (57 million Liters/hour) into the White Water Rapids which then flows over Sahalie Falls and Koosah Falls

evidence.claim: The lake forms the McKenzie River’s headwaters
evidence.quote: Clear Lake is the headwaters of the McKenzie River

evidence.claim: At Proxy Falls, the water’s disappearance is part of the story.
evidence.quote: The water plunges into porous subsoil and sinks underground, giving the impression that there is no outlet on the surface.

evidence.claim: The main drop is 226 feet, descending from a hanging valley shaped by glaciers 6,000 years ago.
evidence.quote: The waterfall is notable for its main drop of 226 feet (69 m)

evidence.claim: descending from a hanging valley shaped by glaciers 6,000 years ago.
evidence.quote: Proxy Falls formed at the end of a hanging valley created by the canyons cut by glaciers 6,000 years ago.

evidence.claim: shaped by glaciers 6,000 years ago.
evidence.quote: Proxy Falls formed at the end of a hanging valley created by the canyons cut by glaciers 6,000 years ago.

evidence.claim: Proxy and Upper Proxy falls plunge from glacier-cut cliffs, with lava fields surrounding them on a valley floor filled by eruptions from nearby cinder cones.
evidence.quote: Proxy Falls and its neighbor, Upper Proxy Falls, plummet off glacier-cut cliffs surrounded by lava fields from cinder cones near North Sister that filled the valley floor.

evidence.claim: The falling water sinks through porous ground, leaving the impression of a pool without a surface outlet.
evidence.quote: The water plunges into porous subsoil and sinks underground, giving the impression that there is no outlet on the surface.

evidence.claim: An unpaved 1.6-mile loop from OR 242 passes through lava fields and conifer forest, with viewpoints toward both waterfalls.
evidence.quote: An unpaved foot trail loops around lava fields and dense conifer forests with viewpoints to Proxy Falls and the smaller Upper Proxy Falls. It starts at the trailhead off highway 242 and totals 1.6 miles of easy hiking.

evidence.claim: Dee Wright Observatory turns rough lava into a frame for the Cascade peaks.
evidence.quote: The viewing windows are cut to specifically highlight the neighboring mountains.

evidence.claim: The open shelter was built with basaltic andesite gathered at the construction site.
evidence.quote: The observatory is an open shelter built with basaltic andesite lava found at the construction site.

evidence.claim: Its viewing holes isolate individual mountains, while a bronze peak finder on the roof helps identify the surrounding summits and geological features.
evidence.quote: There is also a 36 inch (90 cm) diameter, bronze azimuth-like "peak finder" on the observatory’s roof to help visitors locate nearby geologic features as well as the surrounding mountain peaks.

evidence.claim: A Civilian Conservation Corps crew completed the structure in 1935 and named it for its foreman, who had died the previous year.
evidence.quote: It was completed in 1935, and named for the construction crew’s foreman who had died the previous year

evidence.claim: Beside it, the paved half-mile Lava River Interpretive Trail leads through lava gutters and crevasses, with panels explaining their geology.
